5. Appellant contested the suit claiming that the award is not liable to be set aside. The trial court dismissed the suit. Respondent filed F.M.A. No.142 of 1974 in the High Court Division challenging the judgment and order of the trial court. The learned Judges of the High Court Division allowed the appeal holding that the award was void ab-initio since it was made beyond the statutory period of limitation. 

 6. Appellant obtained leave to consider whether the learned Judges of the High Court’s Division were wrong in not holding that the parties waived the period of limitation and contested the arbitration proceeding without asserting the point of limitation till the award was given. 

 7. Mr. A. W. Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong. in their finding on the point of limitation since the period of limitation mentioned in Article 3 of the First Schedule of the Arbitration Act is, in view of the provisions of section 3 of the Act, one of the conditions of the Agreement and could not be compared to a statutory limitation as provided in the Limitation Act or any other statute. He further submitted that the position being so, the parties to the Agreement were at liberty to vary or waive the condition regarding the making of the award within 4 months after entering on the reference etc. as mentioned in Article 3 of the 1st Schedule of the Act. He submitted that both the parties waived the period of limitation and contested the arbitration proceeding without asserting the bar of limitation till the award was made. He also submitted that it was apparent why the respondent did not raise any objection before the Arbitrator on the ground of limitation. According to him, the respondent expected that the award would go in his favour. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submitted that the judgment of the High Court Division was scrappy and did not consider the merits of the case at all. 

 8. It appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division after referring to the provisions of Article 3 of the 1st Schedule of the Arbitration Act and the fact that the award was given beyond four months after the reference was made was unable to accept the finding of the trial court that the parties before Arbitrator had waived the question of limitation and, therefore, the award was not barred by law and came to the conclusion that the award having been given well beyond the statutory period of limitation was void ab-initio. The short ground on which the learned Judges proceeded to set aside the judgment of the trial court would appear from the following observations: 

 10. From a reading of the judgment of the trial court it appears that the objections raised by the respondent to the award as quoted above were discussed and considered by it. The trial court noted that the plaintiff-respondent made the reference on July 10, 1969 but the award was made on October 19, 1970 which was well beyond four months from the date of reference. The learned Subordinate Judge overruled the objection by holding that since the respondent did not raise any objection to the passing of the award after the expiry of four months from the date of reference nor informed the appellant that with the expiry of this period the arbitration proceeding came to an end and he would not be bound by the award if made by the Arbitrator after the date, but on the contrary respondent appeared before the Arbitrator and placed arguments in support of his case. This amounted to waiving the condition regarding the time for passing the award. On the objections regarding the passing of the award by the Additional Secretary instead of the Secretary, Food Department, it was found that the award was made by the latter. As regards the point that the arbitration was beyond the subject matter of reference, the learned Subordinate Judge held that the dispute having arisen on the respective claims of the respondent for the amount of Tk. 94, 521.39 and the appellant for Tk. 1,57,756.25 and that the Arbitrator considered both the claim and counter-claim of the parties it could not be said that the Arbitrator acted beyond the scope of reference. The main contention which arose for our determination was, however, with regard to the period of limitation of four months as mentioned in Article 3 of the 1st Schedule of the Arbitration Act. Its provisions are as follows: 

 11. If the provisions arc interpreted as strictly as any other statutory provisions regarding limitation the appellant would seem to have no ground to stand upon, since it appears that the award was made beyond the period mentioned therein. To get over this difficulty the learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that having regard to section 3 of the Arbitration Act the provisions set out in the First Schedule formed part of the arbitration agreement and as such like any other condition in the agreement they could be waived or departed from by the consent of both the parties to the arbitration agreement. Section 3 of the Act provides as follows: 

 12. From the conduct of the parties to the arbitration agreement, particularly the respondent, it appears that no objection was raised by either of the parties to the arbitration proceeding that the award could not be passed as the period mentioned in Article 3 had already expired, nor did the respondent inform the Arbitrator that he would not be bound by any award since the time for passing it had expired. This should be considered as waiver of the condition regarding limitation for passing the award. In support, the learned Additional Attorney-General cited a few decisions. In Haji Ghulam Mohyuddin V. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1967 Lah. 204, similar point was involved as to whether the award given four months after the arbitrator entered upon the reference was void being in violation of paragraph 3 of the First Schedule of the Arbitration Act. As already seen, its provisions were to be considered as implied terms of the Arbitration agreement as laid down in section 3 of the Act. In observing that the provisions of the First Schedule insofar as they were made the terms of the Arbitration agreement did not acquire a status higher than the other terms of the same, the Court observed:
